title: Crew — proposed next features
subtitle: Nine suggestions drawn from your actual usage: 131 sessions in crew-store.json and five weeks of crew-crash.log. Approve, reject, or ask for changes. Everything autosaves.

groups.name: Gaps the data exposed
groups.dek: Things the numbers say are missing, and that the UI gives no hint of.

groups.name: Lifecycle debt
groups.dek: The store grows forever and has no exit.

groups.dek: Concepts that overlap, or that lump different things together.

items.title: Give a session a working directory when you create it
items.prompt: All 131 sessions in the store have cwd = $HOME, and recentDirs is empty — the directory picker has never been used once. Every agent therefore starts in home and has to be told where the work is, in prose, every single time. Capture a project directory at creation: default to the last directory used for that label, offer recent/starred repos, and infer from the label when it matches a known checkout. Populate recentDirs so the second session in a project is a one-click affair.

meta.Why now: This is the clearest gap the data shows, and it is invisible in the UI: nothing signals that cwd is a thing you were meant to set. Every session pays a prompt-tax to explain where it is.

Done looks like: Session creation captures a directory, defaulting to the last one used for that label
recentDirs is populated and offers recent/starred repos
Existing sessions keep working with cwd=$HOME

items: Shipping a picker that is still skippable by default — the current one already is
Guessing the directory from the label without letting you correct it

items.title: Restore recent sessions eagerly, the rest lazily on click
items.prompt: 98 of 131 sessions arrived in two programmatic bursts (2026-08-19 and 2026-08-26) with median gaps between creations of 0.75s and 0.14s — machine speed, not human. Of the 66 restored on 26 Aug, 54 were never prompted again; of the 32 on 19 Aug, all 32 were never prompted. Restore faithfully rebuilds everything and you then use almost none of it. Your refinement, and it is better than the preview dialog originally proposed: restore eagerly only what was actually prompted in the last week, and leave the rest as lightweight placeholders in the roster that hydrate the moment you click one. No dialog, no decision at startup, nothing lost — the cost simply moves to the sessions you touch.

meta.Why now: Restore is the single biggest source of clutter in the store, and the clutter is what makes every later list, view and grouping feature necessary. Lazy hydration also removes the startup cost entirely, which the preview dialog would not have.
meta.Shape: Your proposal: eager for last-week, lazy-on-click for the rest

Evidence: Creation-gap analysis of crew-store.json; the 36-session set literally named 'Recovered'

Done looks like: Sessions prompted in the last week restore eagerly, as today
Everything else appears in the roster as a placeholder and hydrates on first click
No restore dialog and no decision asked for at startup
A placeholder is visually honest about not being live yet

items: A click that feels slow because hydration is not instant and gives no feedback
Placeholders that look identical to live sessions
Losing scrollback or agent context on a lazily restored session
Hiding the rest instead of actually deferring the work

items.title: Add a real archive, because the store is already 90% archive
items.prompt: 117 of 131 sessions are past the 72-hour staleHideHours cutoff; only 14 are visible. The other 103 are not gone, they are hidden — still loaded, still restored, still in every file write. Hiding was the cheap version of a lifecycle. Add an explicit archive state with its own view, a restore-from-archive path, and a real delete. Then stop loading archived sessions into the live roster at all.

meta.Why now: The store grows forever and has no exit. Hiding masks the symptom while the cost (load, persist, restore) keeps compounding.

Evidence: crew-store.json: 117/131 older than staleHideHours=72; sessions[] has no archived/deleted state

Done looks like: An explicit archived state, separate from stale-hidden
Archived sessions are not loaded into the live roster
A real delete, and a restore-from-archive path

items: Another hiding mechanism layered on the first
Deleting anything without an undo

items.title: Treat standing projects and scratch sessions as different things
items.prompt: Of the 40 sessions ever actually prompted, the split is bimodal: 14 standing projects with a median 27-day life (Crew, Eval Atlas, Portfolio, Work Website, FDE, Groundtruth Mapper, the skill sessions) and 17 same-day throwaways (spec cleanup, Vertical Blog, Rounded Corners Spec). The app treats both identically — same persistence, same restore, same roster weight. Let a session be promoted to a standing project (always restored, always visible, pinned) or marked scratch (never restored, auto-archived at end of day).

meta.Why now: One lifecycle for two species is why the roster needs so much hiding and grouping machinery. Sort it at the source.

Evidence: Lifespan analysis of the 40 prompted sessions: 14 over 7 days, 17 under 1 day

Done looks like: A session can be promoted to standing or marked scratch
Scratch sessions are never restored and auto-archive
The default for a new session needs no decision from you

items: Forcing a lifecycle choice up front at creation
A third grouping concept competing with tags and workspaces

items.title: Offer to resume prior work instead of silently creating a duplicate
items.prompt: 24 sessions share a duplicated label — 'Develop Week In Review App', 'Create Project Tracker Site', 'Fix Icon Positioning Bug' and nine others each exist twice. That is the same job started again, with the earlier session's context stranded. On creation, when a label (or directory) matches an existing session, offer Resume that one as the primary action and Create a new one as the secondary.

meta.Why now: Duplicates are how context gets lost: the work continues but the thread doesn't. The data shows it happening roughly one time in five.

Evidence: crew-store.json: 12 labels occurring twice, covering 24 of 131 sessions

Done looks like: Matching label or directory offers Resume as the primary action
Create new stays available as the secondary
No prompt at all when there is no match

items: A modal on every single session creation
Matching so loosely that unrelated work is offered

items.title: Lean on tags, which you use, rather than workspaces, which you mostly do not
items.prompt: Tags are on 86 of 131 sessions (WORK 24, TOOLS 17, Other 12, FDE 9, Game 8, CREW 7, craft 5, SKILLS 4). Workspaces are assigned on only 43, leaving 88 unassigned, and two of the four workspaces are near-empty (HACK 6, OCTOBER 7). You adopted the lightweight primitive and skipped the heavyweight one. Make tags first-class: filter and group by tag, a saved view per tag, tag colours in the roster — and consider deriving workspaces from tags rather than maintaining both.

meta.Why now: Two overlapping grouping systems, one adopted twice as much as the other. Invest in the one that won.

Evidence: crew-store.json: tag set on 86/131; workspaceIds empty on 88/131

Done looks like: Filter and group the roster by tag
A saved view per tag
A decision recorded on whether workspaces stay

items: Keeping both systems at full cost and calling it choice
Migrating workspaces away without your say-so

items.title: Decide whether custom agents earn their place
items.prompt: All four agents in the store are the seeded builtins (UX Critique, Code Review, Security Review, Doc Writer) and not one custom agent has ever been created. There is exactly one custom view, 'Core Focus'. Either the authoring path is undiscoverable or the need is already met by the four defaults. Before building more agent surface, find out which — then either make authoring reachable from where agents are used, or freeze the feature at four good builtins and spend the room elsewhere.

meta.Why now: This is a build-versus-cut decision, and right now it would be made on vibes. It is also the clearest thing the proposed opt-in tracking would settle.

Evidence: crew-store.json: agents[] all builtin:true; customViews[] length 1

Done looks like: A decision recorded either way, with a reason
If kept: authoring reachable from where agents are used
If cut: the four builtins stay and the surface is frozen

items: Building more agent surface before answering this
Removing the four builtins, which are used

items.title: Add opt-in, local-only usage insights
items.prompt: Flat off by default, with a plain-language consent screen that says exactly what is recorded, and nothing leaves the machine — append-only JSONL in Application Support, viewable in-app, with a one-click wipe. There is no third-party analytics in Crew today and none should be added. Record counters and durations, never prompt or terminal content: session opened/focused/closed, prompts per session, foreground dwell time, which view (grid, focus, custom) is used, agent and conductor invocations, restore accepted versus dismissed, crashes and PTY failures. Ship a 'Your usage' panel that shows you your own numbers, so the feature pays the user back rather than only paying us.

meta.Why now: The analysis behind CB-13 to CB-19 had to be reverse-engineered from two timestamps per session, and several questions were simply unanswerable: how long you actually work in a session, how many prompts it takes, which views you use, whether a session ended satisfied or abandoned. The memory census that exists ran on exactly one day (26 Aug) and the crash log has recorded 19 clean quits and zero crashes, so what instrumentation there is tells us almost nothing about use.

Evidence: No analytics dependency anywhere in src/; crew-crash.log: 1289 memcensus samples all on 2026-08-26, 19 quits, 0 crashes

Done looks like: Off by default, with plain-language consent naming what is recorded
Append-only JSONL in Application Support; nothing leaves the machine
In-app viewer and a one-click wipe
Counters and durations only — never prompt or terminal content

items: Any third-party analytics SDK
On by default, or consent buried in settings
Recording prompt text, file paths or terminal output
Collecting data with no user-visible payback

items.title: Stop treating memory and stability as the next performance problem
items.prompt: The census recorded a JS heap of 15-28 MB against a 3586 MB limit, peak DOM 1681 nodes, and the crash log holds 19 clean quits with zero crashes across five weeks. Whatever is worth fixing next, it is not footprint or stability. Record this as a deliberate negative result so the next perf instinct gets checked against it, and re-measure only with a census that runs on more than one day and more than one tile.

meta.Why now: Perf work is the easiest thing to start and the hardest to justify. The only measurement available says there is nothing here.

Evidence: crew-crash.log: heapMB 15-28 of heapLimitMB 3586; 0 crashes, 19 quits, Aug 26 - Oct 3

Done looks like: The negative result is written down where the next perf instinct will meet it
Any re-measure runs across more than one day and more than one tile

items: Starting footprint work anyway on instinct
Treating one day of single-tile data as proof for all configurations
